name: Manichaean dualism and Augustine's rejection of it
plain_explanation: Before converting to Catholic Christianity, Augustine was a Manichaean, believing evil to be a real, material substance opposed to good; he abandoned this partly because Manichaean astronomical teachings did not match what he had learned from real astronomers.
precise_definition: The Manichaean doctrine, held by Augustine for roughly a decade, that evil is a positive substance and that some other 'nature' within a person, rather than the person's own will, is responsible for sin; Augustine's rejection was driven partly by an early, distinctively scientific dissatisfaction (Manichaean astronomical claims about solstices, equinoxes, and eclipses failed to match established astronomical calculation), and later by his coming to believe, against Manichaean dualism, that evil originates not from a substance but from 'perverseness of will.'
why_it_mattered: It marks Augustine's transition from a materialist, dualist metaphysics to a will-centered account of evil that becomes central to Christian orthodoxy and to his mature theology (Chapter IV).
historical_origin: Documented in Confessions Books III-VII, including his disappointing encounter with the Manichaean bishop Faustus, who candidly admitted ignorance of astronomy.
examples: Augustine's comparison of Manichaean cosmology with 'the best astronomers' and finding it wanting
Faustus's frank admission of ignorance, which Augustine found appealing despite it costing Faustus intellectual credibility
competing_positions: Academic skepticism, which briefly attracted Augustine in Rome before his conversion
influence_on_later_thinkers: Underpins Augustine's account of the will and moral responsibility developed at length in Chapter IV.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: A purely intellectual/religious transition, though it shapes Augustine's subsequent controversialist writing against Manichaeism as bishop.
